newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African Zulu party sets out constitution demands.
newsitem.headline: S.African Zulu party sets out constitution demands.

text.p: South African negotiators racing to beat an October 11 deadline to correct a draft post-apartheid constitution notched up their first success on Wednesday, but new demands by conservative Zulus could still cause delays.
An all-party sub-committee agreed to toughen up the rules for changing the constitution, which the top-ranking Constitutional Court last month said needed some amendments.

Its proposal that amendments should need consent from between two-thirds and 75 percent of all members of parliament will be put to the 490-member Constitutional Assembly (CA) for ratification next week.

But at the same meeting, Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's traditionalist Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) proposed amendments to 40 of the 244 clauses of the draft constitution, which the government plans to put into effect on January 1 next year.
The IFP rejoined the constitution-writing process on Tuesday, after an 18-month boycott triggered by a row with the ruling African National Congress (ANC).
The IFP accused the ANC of reneging on an agreement that drew Buthelezi into the country's first democratic elections in April 1994 and walked out of the CA in February last year.
IFP strategist Walter Felgate told Reuters the amendments could make the constitution acceptable to millions of rural blacks and many of the country's 8.5 million Zulu tribesmen.
"We're talking about a way in which we can democratise local government and at the same time give tribal councils and traditional leaders a meaningful role in the process.
"Throughout Africa there have been enormous mistakes made by eliminating traditional leaders from local government and we're trying to avoid that," he said.
The changes proposed by the IFP would swing the balance of power over the nine provinces and more than 800 municipalities away from the central government towards the provinces.

"We want to restore the balance of provincial competence over local government matters. The balance has swung now in favour of the national government. We want to restore the balance so that it is concurrent, so that we can equally decide on it," said IFP negotiator Peter Smith.
The IFP proposals for greater provincial autonomy will reopen one of the major debates of the two-year negotiations leading to the adoption of the draft constitution on May 8.
